1.pericope_label: We sent Timotheus, our brother and minister of God

schools.summary: The chapter's first difficulty is historical, so meet it head on: Acts never places Timothy at Athens, yet this letter says he was sent from there. Give the reconstruction and the reason for it -- the tense of "to be left" requires an actual parting with somebody, so it cannot mean merely enduring loneliness a while longer, and the stay in Athens was made expressly to wait for the companions, while the departure was unhurried. Conclude that they joined him and were sent back almost at once. Then the words: the verb of forbearing comes from the noun for a roof and covers concealing, keeping off and enduring; and most of the best editors judge the description of Timothy interpolated, reading instead "our brother, and God's fellow-worker in the gospel." Ask why so familiar a man is described at all, and answer that he probably carried the letter.

Put the whole weight on the word "alone," because that is where the argument lies. Timothy was the most faithful companion he had and at that moment the only one, so that being without him was inconvenient and distressing; that he chose to be left by himself rather than leave this congregation deserted is the proof of affection the passage exists to give. Draw the second consequence too, that in sending such a man he lends authority to the teaching they had received from him, so that it may remain the more deeply impressed. On the title "brother," ground it in a shared household rather than an office -- the same heavenly Father, the same family, a friendship sticking closer than brethren commonly do.

Open by stating the motive plainly: no report could be had without sending a messenger express, and he preferred sending one to remaining in uncertainty. Then use the description of Timothy as an occasion to talk about ministry. He was a youth when converted and is elsewhere called a son, yet is called brother here; minister of God means employed by God to preach, which was God's work, and the primitive preachers were his workmen and laboured in that calling. Press the application without softening it -- there were no sinecures then, it is the same still, and the question is who works. Note also that the plural at the opening covers more than one man.

Make the sending itself the lesson before touching the words. Though Timothy was very useful to him and could not well be spared, he was content for their good to be left alone; and those ministers do not duly value the establishment and welfare of their people who cannot deny themselves in many things to that end. Then take the titles in order. Timothy was junior in age, inferior in gifts and graces, of a lower rank in the ministry -- an evangelist where the writer was an apostle -- and is still called brother, which is humility and a desire to put honour on him before the churches. Add what follows for ministers generally: they are labourers in the Lord's vineyard with an honourable office and hard work, and should strengthen one another's hands rather than strive and contend, which only hinders the work.

debates.question: Who is meant by "we could no longer forbear"?

sides.position: The writer alone, by the limitation two chapters earlier and the outright singular three verses later
Either the literary plural or, more likely, the writer and Silas
Paul and Silvanus
Paul, Silas and Timothy, who had borne the longing together like an insupportable burden

debates.question: Was Timothy ever at Athens, given that Acts does not place him there?

sides.position: He must have been: the tense of "to be left" absolutely necessitates an act of parting with someone, so both companions joined him at Athens and were sent back almost at once, Silas into Macedonia and Timothy to Thessalonica
He was, and three circumstances make it probable: a message was sent back for them to come at once, the stay in Athens was made in order to wait for them, and the departure was unhurried
Both came to Athens, Timothy was sent right back to Thessalonica, and Silas was despatched later; then both came from Macedonia to Corinth
They were summoned to Athens and most likely came; Timothy was then sent back, and the writer went on to Corinth, where Timothy rejoined him

outliers.note: Alone works out at length the conflict between this passage and the narrative of Acts, arguing from the tense of "to be left" that the phrase absolutely requires an act of parting with somebody and cannot mean merely enduring loneliness longer, and alone accounts for the silence of Acts about the despatch of Silas from Athens by observing that it held no interest for the readers of this letter.

Alone puts the whole weight on the word "alone," observing that Timothy was the most faithful companion the writer had and at that moment the only one, so that doing without him was distressing, and that choosing to be left by himself rather than leave this congregation deserted is the proof of affection the passage exists to give; he adds that sending such a man also lends authority to the teaching they had received from him.

Alone turns the phrase "minister of God" into a rebuke of his own day, observing that preaching the gospel was God's work and the primitive preachers were his workmen who laboured in that calling -- there were no sinecures then, it is the same still, and the question is who works.

themes: Wherefore when we could no longer forbear, we thought it good to be left at Athens alone
And sent Timotheus, our brother, and minister of God, and our fellowlabourer in the gospel of Christ

3.pericope_label: No man moved by these afflictions; lest the tempter have tempted you

schools.summary: The verb rendered "moved" occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and its history is worth giving: properly to wag, as a dog wags its tail in fondness, then to fawn or flatter or wheedle, and only then to waver from dread. Say which end of that range you take and why -- "seduced" or "beguiled" keeps the metaphor, while the familiar rendering leans on a variant reading found in two manuscripts and in the papyri. Correct the preposition as well: the afflictions are those the readers are in the midst of, chiefly their own rather than the writer's. On being appointed to them, be honest that the pronoun's reference is not fixed, and note that the general sense serves the argument best, since it shows this congregation had received only the common lot.

Preach persecution as the terms of the calling, not as an accident of it. There is no reason believers should be dismayed at it as though it were new and unusual, since this is the condition assigned us and we are Christians on that condition; and because they had been forewarned, they were bound to fight the more bravely. Add the second reason the forewarning was given: incessant afflictions made the apostle contemptible among rude and ignorant people, so he points out that nothing had befallen him which he had not foretold. Then handle the tempter. Temptations are always to be dreaded, since it is Satan's proper office to tempt and he never ceases laying snares; and note that the writer now says openly what at the outset he avoided as too harsh, his fear that the labour had been wasted.

Refuse the strong construction of "appointed" and say why. God appoints nothing of this kind, but permits it, having made man a free agent; what the words assert is that we are exposed to such things and that they are unavoidable as the world now stands. Keep the rest short and practical: to be moved means to apostatise from Christianity, and the forewarning was given because it is according to the nature of wicked men to persecute the followers of God. On the sending, state the fear exactly as it stood -- knowing they would be persecuted and knowing that apostasy was possible, he sent to learn whether they stood, lest they had been tempted to consult their present ease and abandon the gospel.

Raise the question the passage invites and nobody else asks. How is it that a man who heard unutterable words and was caught up to the third heaven did not know how matters stood at Thessalonica, when the distance was small and the parting had been short? Do not evade it. Answer that the saints did not know all things, and prove it from three cases: Elisha, who did not know what ailed the woman; Elijah, who said he only was left and was told of seven thousand; and Samuel, sent to anoint and warned not to look on the countenance nor the height of the stature, because man looks on the outward appearance and God on the heart.

debates.question: What does the verb rendered "moved" mean here?

sides.position: To be so agitated by the terror of persecution as to forsake one's religion; the word means properly to wag, as dogs wag their tails in fondness, then to fawn or flatter, then to waver from dread
Seduced: the fawning of an animal on its master, then wheedling, then the gradual detachment of a person from his resolution by insinuating representations, whether of flattery or of fear
Beguiled; the sense of "moved" or troubled rests on a different reading found in two manuscripts and in the papyri
Caused to apostatise from Christianity

debates.question: Whose afflictions are meant, and in what sense are we appointed to them?

sides.position: Chiefly the readers' own, not the writer's; the preposition should be "in" or "in the midst of" rather than "by." The pronoun covers all Christian people, and election into the church is an election to suffering
The writer's own, endured in preaching among them, and feared to be what might shake young converts
It is the condition on which we are Christians at all, assigned by the Lord, so persecution is neither new nor unusual and the forewarned should fight the more bravely
God appoints nothing of this kind but permits it, having made man a free agent; the words mean only that we lie open to such things and they are unavoidable
The reference cannot be fixed -- it may be the writer, the writer with his readers, or Christians at large -- and the general sense serves the argument best

outliers.note: Alone raises the question the sending invites: how a man who had heard unutterable words and been caught up to the third heaven did not know how matters stood at Thessalonica, when the distance was small and the parting short. He answers that the saints did not know all things and proves it from three cases -- Elisha, who did not know what ailed the woman; Elijah, who said he only was left and was told of seven thousand; and Samuel, warned not to look on the countenance nor the height of the stature.

Alone refuses the strong sense of "we are appointed thereunto," holding that God appoints nothing of this kind but permits it, having made man a free agent, and rendering the clause as meaning only that we lie open to such things and they are unavoidable in the present state of the world.

Alone corrects the preposition so as to change whose sufferings are in view, holding that the afflictions are those the readers are in the midst of rather than the writer's, and alone observes that the original leaves no doubt the readers had been tempted, the only doubt being how they bore it.

themes: That no man should be moved by these afflictions: for yourselves know that we are appointed thereunto
For verily, when we were with you, we told you before that we should suffer tribulation
For this cause... I sent to know your faith, lest by some means the tempter have tempted you

6.pericope_label: Timothy's good tidings; now we live if ye stand fast; praying night and day

schools.summary: Note first that the verb used of Timothy's report is the ordinary word for preaching the gospel, here applied to news about a congregation -- an enthusiastic word, and worth remarking on. Then settle the place: Timothy came to Corinth, which means this letter was not written from Athens as its subscription asserts. Distinguish the two graces reported: the confidence in God that enabled them to endure, and the tenderness with which they carried one another through; and read the "good remembrance" as kind rather than merely vivid, since a congregation beginning to fall away would not have wished to see its teachers. On the adverb of praying, build it up as it is built: one word meaning abundantly, a second out of bounds, a third more than out of bounds. The verb for supplying what is lacking is a mending word, used of nets and of men.

Take the circumstances into account or the passage loses its force: he was in the midst of distress, where there might have seemed no room for cheerfulness, and the news carries him out of it into joy. Give the sentence its own words -- though in myself I am dead, yet in your welfare I live -- and then make it a standard for pastors, who ought to reckon themselves happy when the church prospers though they are otherwise encompassed with miseries, and to pine with grief when the building they raised decays though all else goes well. On the prayer for what is lacking, state the rule it implies: we may never congratulate men in this life so unqualifiedly as to stop desiring something better for them, since they are still on the road and may fall back, and those who far surpass others are still far from the goal.

Number the good tidings in three, since that is how they come: they stood fast in the faith, they loved one another and lived in unity, and they remained affectionately attached to their teacher. Then let the response be as warm as the source is. His afflictions and persecutions seemed trifles when he heard of their perseverance; their steadfastness gave him new life, and he felt that he lived to some purpose because his labour in the Lord was not in vain. Ask the question the passage forces on any preacher: what is it to have preached often, laboured hard and suffered much, if souls are not converted -- and what are conversions worth if those who embraced the gospel do not walk steadily and persevere? End on the prayer, mingled with all his other prayers, that he might be given opportunity to fill up what their instruction still lacked.

Dwell on the mutuality, because that is what the passage actually reports. Their love to the gospel and to its ministers continued; the names of their teachers were dear to them and they greatly desired to see them again -- and there was no love lost, for the apostle was as desirous to see them. Say that it is happy where there is such mutual love between minister and people, since it promotes religion and the success of the gospel; and give the reason plainly, that the world hates them both, and therefore they should love one another.

sides.position: From Corinth, not Athens as the subscription asserts: Timothy came to the writer at Corinth and the letter was sent as soon as he arrived
From Corinth, Timothy having come there after his mission, as Acts relates
Timothy had already returned from Thessalonica, and the occasion of the letter is the relief at the news he brought

The new life and vigour the news infused, contrasted with the deadly sinking felt at the thought of their apostasy; the conditional has a half-future sense, the continuance of that life hanging on their steadfastness
They had been dead men, lifeless and disconsolate, carrying about the dying of the Lord Jesus, and the news was like life from the dead
Though in myself I am dead, yet in your welfare I live -- the standard by which all pastors should measure their connection with the church
Life in the sense of the Latin epigram, that living consists not in mere existence but in health and enjoyment
Their steadfastness gives new life and comfort, and the feeling of having lived to some purpose

outliers.note: Alone draws from Timothy's arrival at Corinth the conclusion that this letter was not written from Athens as its own subscription asserts, but from Corinth, the letter being sent as soon as the report was made.

Alone reads the joy against the writer's circumstances, that he was in the midst of distress where there might have seemed no room for cheerfulness, and alone turns the declaration into a standard for pastors -- that they should reckon themselves happy when the church prospers though otherwise encompassed with miseries, and pine with grief when the building they raised decays though all else goes well.

Alone reads the question about thanks as an apology for the extravagant language of the three preceding verses, alone reports and rejects a rival construction making both pronouns of "now we live" general, and alone explains the vehemence of the praying by the belief that the obstacle was the adversary's and not God's will, since the essence of prayer is to conform the will to God's.
Alone builds the adverb of praying out of its parts, one word meaning abundantly, a second out of bounds and this third more than out of bounds, so that all bounds overflow.

themes: But now when Timotheus came from you unto us, and brought us good tidings of your faith and charity
For now we live, if ye stand fast in the Lord
Night and day praying exceedingly that we might see your face, and might perfect that which is lacking in your faith

11.pericope_label: God direct our way; the Lord make you increase in love; stablish your hearts

schools.summary: This is a theologically loaded passage and the grammar carries the load, so show it. Two subjects are named, the Father and the Lord Jesus, and the verb of directing is singular. Report that some argue from this for the substantial unity of the Son with the Father, and enter the caution: it must not be pressed so far as to imply a unity of person, though the wish plainly assumes their equality and the plural verb would have been unthinkable. Note the article covering the first pair of titles and standing again before the name of Jesus, and that a third-person optative of wish is almost unknown elsewhere in the New Testament. On the closing company, say whether you take it of angels, of the redeemed, or of both -- and note that the Greek hints these are to sit as assessors in the judgment.

Begin from the obstruction: he prays that the Lord, having removed Satan's hindrance, may open a door and be the leader of his way. The doctrine underneath is that we cannot move a step to any purpose except under God's guidance, and that when he holds out his hand it is to no purpose that Satan tries to turn our course. Note that the same office is assigned to God and to Christ, which teaches that Christ has divinity and power in common with the Father. On "the Lord" of the next verse, it is worth arguing that the Spirit is meant, so that Father, Son and Spirit are all addressed here, the Spirit being God equally and therefore a fit object of prayer. Then take "hearts" as the innermost part of the soul, and meet the objection: if we stand at the judgment seat by holiness, what is left for pardon to do? Answer that pardon is presupposed, faith coming first as a foundation before a building.

Keep this practical and let the doctrine sit inside it. He was employed in God's work and dared not consult his own inclinations, but looked for continual direction where, when and how to do his Master's work -- that is what asking God to direct a journey means. On the love, note that they already had enough of it to unite them in one body, and that what is asked is increase and abundance, that they might feel toward each other what he felt for them all. Then make love the ground of stability: without love to God and man there is no establishment in the religion of Christ, for it is love that produces both solidity and continuance, and he who is filled with it is unblameable in holiness because love is the fulfilling of the law. Close on the coming, and press it -- every hour that passes advances his approach, and when the soul departs the body, that is the coming of the Lord to us.

Take the prayer as the answer to a question the chapter has raised: how a teacher at a distance can still do his people good. He desired their faith to be perfected and could not himself be the author of it, pretending to no dominion over their faith, and so he concludes with prayer. Then observe whom the prayer is addressed to, and do not hurry past it. Prayer is a part of religious worship and all religious worship is due to God only; here it is offered to the Father, and offered also to our Lord Jesus Christ -- therefore Jesus Christ our Lord is God, even as God our Father is God. Prayer is not merely offered in the name of Christ but offered up to Christ himself as Lord and Saviour. Add the small honest note that a journey looks like the sort of thing a man settles by his own will, and that this one was nevertheless taken to God.

debates.question: What follows from the singular verb with two subjects?

sides.position: Some divines argue from it for the substantial unity of the Son with the Father; it must not be pressed so far as to imply a personal unity, but it does imply their equality, and the plural would have been unthinkable
Unity in the Godhead; note also one article covering the first pair of titles and a separate article before the name of Jesus
Prayer is religious worship and worship is due to God only; a prayer offered to Christ therefore makes Christ God as the Father is God
It is a real prayer to the Lord Jesus, and shows that it is right to worship him -- the writer would not have prayed to an angel to direct his way
The same office is assigned to God and to Christ because the Father confers no blessing except through Christ's hand, which teaches that Christ has divinity and power in common with him

debates.question: Who is "the Lord" in the twelfth verse?

sides.position: The Spirit, so that Father, Son and Spirit are all addressed across these verses; the Spirit is God equally with them and therefore a fit object of prayer, which otherwise he would not be
The Lord Jesus, the name by which he is commonly designated; this is a petition to him as the fountain of all grace
Not the Son only; the word here appears to be an equivalent for the name of God

debates.question: Who are the saints who come with him?

sides.position: Both the attending angels and the whole number of the redeemed
Probably not the angels, though the word could be stretched to cover them, but those spoken of a chapter later; the Greek seems almost to indicate they are to be assessors in the judgment
The term is used to admonish us that we are called by Christ to be gathered with them, which ought to whet our desire for holiness

outliers.note: Alone takes "the Lord" of the twelfth verse to be the Spirit, and does so in order to establish that Father, Son and Spirit are all addressed in this prayer, the Spirit being God equally with them and therefore a fit object of prayer, which otherwise he would not be.

Alone raises the objection that if we stand at the judgment seat by holiness there is nothing left for the remission of sins to do, and answers it, that pardon is not excluded but presupposed, faith by which God is pacified toward us coming first as the foundation comes before the building.

Alone reports that some argue from the singular verb for the substantial unity of the Son with the Father while cautioning that it must not be pressed into a unity of person, and alone reads the Greek of the closing clause as hinting that the saints who come with him are to sit as assessors in the judgment.

Alone presses the coming as a personal reckoning, observing that every hour advances its approach and that when the soul departs the body that is the coming of the Lord to us, and alone makes love the cause of stability, since it is love that produces both solidity and continuance.

themes: Now God himself and our Father, and our Lord Jesus Christ, direct our way unto you
And the Lord make you to increase and abound in love one toward another, and toward all men
To the end he may stablish your hearts unblameable in holiness before God... at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ with all his saints
